details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: The priority list contains 'Throughput' three times instead of ranking the three defined KPIs (resource_efficiency, operator_fatigue, noise_level) — what is the intended priority ordering among these three objectives when they conflict?
flags.resolution: Priority set to resource_efficiency > operator_fatigue > noise_level, reflecting the manager's stated primary intent of efficiency improvement with ergonomic safety as secondary guardrails.

flags.question: There is no cap on how aggressively the optimiser can push resource efficiency — should a maximum production rate multiplier (e.g. ≤ 1.25× baseline cycle rate) or an energy consumption ceiling (e.g. ≤ 10% above prior-shift energy use) be enforced to prevent the optimiser from trading safety headroom for efficiency gains?
flags.resolution: Apply a soft ceiling of 1.20× prior-shift energy consumption and 1.15× baseline cycle rate; efficiency gains beyond these bounds are rejected unless all hard constraints remain satisfied with ≥10% margin.

flags.field: operator_fatigue hard constraint vs. resource_efficiency maximize
flags.question: Maximising efficiency typically increases workload intensity and fatigue accumulation — at what point in the shift should the fatigue index be evaluated (e.g. end-of-shift average, rolling 30-minute peak, or any instantaneous reading), and is the 0.4 limit a hard ceiling at every measurement interval or only at shift end?
flags.resolution: Fatigue limit of 0.4 is enforced as a rolling 30-minute average throughout the shift; an instantaneous reading may not exceed 0.55 to provide a safety buffer before the hard constraint is breached.

flags.question: Is the 80 dB(A) noise limit a time-weighted average (TWA) over the full shift per ISO 9612, or an instantaneous ceiling that must never be exceeded — since transient high-noise operations (e.g. press cycles) routinely peak above 80 dB(A) even when the shift TWA is compliant?
flags.resolution: Interpreted as an 8-hour TWA per ISO 9612; instantaneous peaks up to 85 dB(A) are permitted provided they do not exceed 15 minutes cumulative duration, consistent with standard industrial hearing-protection guidelines.

flags.question: Without a minimum acceptable efficiency gain, the optimiser may accept a trivially small improvement (e.g. +0.1%) while aggressively consuming constraint headroom — what is the minimum improvement over the prior-shift baseline that constitutes a meaningful target (e.g. ≥5%, ≥10%)?
flags.resolution: A minimum efficiency gain of 5% over the prior-shift normalised baseline is required for the schedule to be accepted; solutions below this floor are treated as infeasible and trigger a fallback to the prior-shift schedule.

details.trigger: Contract deployed; system enters autonomous monitoring

details.detail: All guards satisfied -- S1 metrics within safe bounds

l4_llm_attributions.assumption: Planned throughput rate (UPH) exceeded actual production rate
l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: The schedule S1 was authored assuming a baseline throughput of approximately 32 UPH. Actual throughput in Phase 2 is 28.9 UPH, a ~9.7% shortfall. At this reduced rate, the cumulative units produced per time window fall below the contracted delivery curve, directly eroding the DeadlineGap margin. With margin at only 0.555, the buffer between projected completion and the hard deadline is critically thin — any further throughput degradation or unplanned micro-stoppage will flip this to a negative (missed) margin.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Immediately verify root cause of throughput shortfall (operator count, machine cycle time, queue starvation). If operator absence is confirmed, invoke workload rebalancing or authorize overtime. If a machine is throttled, escalate to maintenance. Target recovery to ≥31 UPH within the next 10 minutes to restore a safe DeadlineGap buffer.

l4_llm_attributions.assumption: Operator staffing level assumed at full complement
l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Operator absence redistributes manual handling and inspection tasks across remaining staff. This increases per-operator cycle time and introduces micro-idle gaps at workstations awaiting human intervention. Even though fatigue_index (0.2996) has not yet breached its own threshold, the increased per-operator workload is suppressing throughput below plan. The compounding effect is a widening gap between work completed and work scheduled, which manifests as the observed DeadlineGap margin of 0.555 — dangerously close to a hard breach.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Cross-train a nearby operator or pull from an adjacent cell immediately. If no backup is available, trigger a partial line rebalance: shift lower-complexity manual tasks to automated assist stations to preserve throughput without further fatiguing the reduced crew. Notify shift supervisor within 2 minutes.

l4_llm_attributions.assumption: Ambient demand load (units in queue) matched contracted schedule volume
l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: A moderate demand surge (estimated ~5.5% above contracted volume) has added unscheduled units to the production queue. Even at unchanged cycle times, the additional queue depth extends the total work horizon beyond the scheduled completion window. With throughput already running below plan, the dual pressure of more units and slower production rate is multiplicative on deadline risk. Energy consumption at 373 kWh is slightly elevated, consistent with extended machine run time attempting to absorb excess queue load.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Audit the current queue depth against the S1 contracted volume. If excess units are confirmed, flag the demand overage to the planning layer and negotiate a partial deadline extension or offload excess units to schedule S2. Do not allow operators to absorb the surge through pace acceleration — this risks fatigue threshold breach in Phase 3.

details.rationale: No feasible candidate exists in the non-dominated front. Returning 'S2d_det' (highest V/R = 0.467) as a fallback; manual review required before deployment.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: Robot R1 runs at the highest speed fraction (0.95) and is the dominant noise emitter. Noise scales approximately linearly with spindle/drive speed in this operating range. Reducing R1 speed by ~5.3% yields an estimated noise reduction of ~4–5 dB (84 × 0.90/0.95 ≈ 79.6 dB), bringing noise below the 80 dB hard limit. This is the smallest single-parameter change that addresses the binding noise violation. Lower robot speed also reduces pacing pressure on the operator, providing a small secondary reduction in fatigue index.

Operator fatigue index (0.5066) must reach ≤0.40 — a required reduction of ~21%. Fatigue accumulates proportionally with human cycle rate. Scaling proportionally: 0.5066 × (0.88/1.05) ≈ 0.424, which approaches but does not fully clear the limit alone; combined with the reduced robot pacing from adjustment 1 (which removes ~2–3% indirect fatigue load from operator synchronization), the composite result should bring fatigue index to approximately 0.39–0.41. This is the smallest multiplier value that, in combination with the speed reduction, reliably clears the 0.40 ceiling.

Adding 4 s of inter-cycle buffer time provides the operator with additional micro-recovery intervals, reducing cumulative fatigue accumulation per shift. This acts as a safety margin for the fatigue constraint, guarding against edge-case variation in actual cycle duration. It also smooths pipeline utilization, reducing burst-loading events that can transiently spike both fatigue and noise. The throughput impact is modest: at 40.5 UPH baseline, a 4 s buffer increase reduces theoretical max throughput by roughly 3–4%, staying well above typical production targets.

details.trigger: Autonomous replan failed; escalation to human manager

details.conflict: A 25.0% surge in production demand has rendered the current schedule infeasible. Two human-centric constraints are simultaneously violated: (1) Operator Fatigue Index reached 0.5066, exceeding the safety ceiling of 0.40 by a margin of +0.1066 — a 26.7% overage that poses ergonomic and safety risks to floor personnel; (2) Ambient Noise Level reached 84.0 dB, exceeding the occupational health limit of 80.0 dB by 4.0 dB — a threshold linked to long-term hearing damage under sustained exposure. Because both violations are human-welfare constraints governed by the CBPA framework's non-negotiable layer, automated scheduling has been halted. Human authority is required to select a remediation path before production can resume.
options: Option 1 — Expand Labor Capacity via Supplemental Shift (Recommended)
Option 2 — Partial Demand Deferral (~10% to Next Planning Cycle)
Option 3 — Temporary Controlled Constraint Relaxation with Compensatory Controls (Last Resort)

details.trigger: Manager decision received; system resumes autonomous execution

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% with dual critical violations (FatigueIndex at 100%, Noise at 80%) under a +25% demand surge indicates the current policy family is fundamentally misaligned. MICRO tweaks (±5% speed, ±10% cycle rate) cannot resolve fatigue violations that are already at 100% probability — increasing throughput to meet demand surge would worsen both fatigue and noise simultaneously. Prior learning strongly corroborates this: both prior similar situations rejected S2 (the current or similar policy) and accepted S3, indicating a policy family switch to S3 (likely a more robust, worker-protective scheduling policy) is the validated solution. MACRO full replanning is not yet warranted as the disturbance is a demand surge (a known disturbance type) and a proven policy exists (S3) that has historically resolved it.
details.reasoning_key_insight: Prior experience provides a clear signal: S2 rejected twice, S3 accepted twice in analogous situations. Switch to the S3 policy family (robust/worker-protective) to simultaneously address fatigue and noise constraints rather than attempting parameter micro-adjustments that cannot overcome 100% fatigue violation probability at current operational bounds.

experience_synthesis.pattern: demand_surge consistently triggers rejection of S2 due to deterministic ergonomic violations (Fatigue > 0.4, Noise > 80dB); S3 is the reliable fallback policy across all observed instances
experience_synthesis.insight: S2 is deterministically excluded for demand_surge scenarios — both rejections cite identical hard constraints (Fatigue > 0.4, Noise > 80dB), so this is a structural incompatibility, not stochastic. S3 satisfies feasibility in 100% of observed cases (n=2), but outcome quality is variable: throughput_uph ranges 24.8–32.6 (~24% spread) and deadline_gap_pct ranges 37.3–52.3 (~40% spread), suggesting S3 is safe but not optimally tuned for demand magnitude. With only 2 samples, the policy direction (avoid S2, use S3) is high-confidence, but the metric ranges should be treated as wide priors pending more data.
